I registered samstevenm.com and samstevenm.net at 1&1 in May 2009. The company
became IONOS somewhere along the way, the hosting contract became an "Expert"
plan, and the bill crept to $18.45 a month once a "PHP 8.1 Extended Support"
surcharge landed this spring. That's about $221 a year for a webspace I hadn't
touched in a decade and two domains I could host anywhere. The rest of our
domains already live at Namecheap with mail at Fastmail, so with the contract
renewal twelve days out, we moved these last two. The whole thing ran in one
afternoon: archive in the morning, DNS and mail cutover after lunch, registrar
transfers confirmed before dinner.

The order of operations is the whole post. Archive first, inventory second,
build the new zone before touching the old one, transfer before you cancel
anything. Do it in that order and there's no outage and nothing lost. Do it in
the other order and you find out what was on that server after it's gone.

## Step 1: Pull everything down

Before changing a single record we mirrored the entire webspace over SFTP:
4,365 files, about 2 GB, into an immutable archive folder that our restic
backups cover. Then we curated. About 400 MB of it turned out to be genuinely
irreplaceable: my dad's project spreadsheets from the original Diligent
Services Inc era with his own job-numbering system, a Lutron Vive parser I
wrote with 226 parsed hub reports, the recorded plat and survey for the house
we owned in Washington during my Navy years, every resume I wrote in 2014,
scans of my service records. Seventeen years of a personal webspace is an
accidental family archive. It's now filed where our internal search actually
indexes it.

The lesson: the webspace is the part of a hosting contract you can't re-buy.
DNS records can be rebuilt from a dig. The files cannot. Mirror first, verify
the copy, then proceed.

## Step 2: Read what you just downloaded

This is the step people skip, and it's where the surprises were. In that
17-year-old webspace we found:

- **An actual malware webshell**, complete with a "with love from moscow"
  string, that fetched and executed a payload from an anonymous gist. The old
  shared host had been compromised at some point. An IONOS console note later
  corroborated it: an abuse ticket from 2018, "Password compromised," on the
  main SFTP user.
- **Live-looking credentials hardcoded in forgotten PHP**: an old MySQL
  database password, a Nest integration with a Google account password and API
  key in plaintext, and a gate page in front of a still-working Dropbox share.

None of that came anywhere near the curated archive; it stays quarantined in
the raw mirror, and every credential goes through a verify-dead-or-rotate
pass. If you're leaving a host you've been on since the 2000s, assume there
are skeletons and go looking for them deliberately. Canceling the contract
doesn't rotate a password you reused somewhere else in 2012.

## Step 3: Inventory before you touch anything

An external `whois` and `dig` pass got us most of the picture: registrar
locks (one domain already unlocked, one not), identical DNS zones on both
domains, MX still live at IONOS. That last one matters. Live MX means real
mailboxes, and mailboxes gate everything, because the moment you cancel the
contract they're gone.

Then a ten-minute walk through the IONOS console, signed in, filled in what
the outside view can't show:

- **Mail topology.** Eleven addresses that turned out to be six real
  mailboxes plus five forwards. The forwards were already pointing off-IONOS;
  the six mailboxes needed import targets at Fastmail.
- **DKIM records the external dig missed.** Three selector CNAMEs that never
  show up unless you know to probe for them. The console zone export is the
  truth; a blind dig is a guess.
- **The included-domain trap.** Both domains were "included" in the hosting
  contract. Cancel the contract first and the domains go down with it.
  Transfers complete first, cancellation last. This ordering is not optional.
- **Contract reality.** Renewal date, monthly line items, which SFTP users
  and databases existed. All of it screenshotted into our ops log before
  anything changed.

## Step 4: Build the new zone before you flip the old one

The cutover trick that makes this a zero-outage move: we built the complete
final zone at Namecheap's FreeDNS before repointing anything. Ten records per
domain, including the old web A records exactly as they were, plus Fastmail's
MX pair, SPF, three DKIM CNAMEs, and DMARC. Mail was pointed at Fastmail only
in the new zone. There was no intermediate state where the old zone got a
Fastmail MX or the new zone still had IONOS mail; one flip, one mail cutover,
no double transition.

Fastmail's side was ready first: both domains added, catch-alls routing every
one of those eleven legacy addresses into accounts we actually read. Then the
nameserver repoint at IONOS. The pleasant surprise: IONOS's old nameservers
keep answering after you repoint, so cached resolvers never went dark while
Namecheap's verification ran. FreeDNS came alive about 42 minutes after the
flip and the public zones matched our build exactly.

## Step 5: Transfer, then repoint the web, then cancel

With DNS serving from the new home, the registrar transfers were the easy
part: unlock, EPP codes, about $24 for both domains, and the transfers
confirmed the same afternoon. `whois` said Namecheap for both before the day
ended, and because .com/.net transfers carry the expiry with them, we keep the
year we'd already paid for.

Then the part we'd actually been waiting to do: the web A records pointing at
IONOS parking got deleted, and both apexes now alias to the family server
that already hosts our other sites. The old site answers from our own nginx
now.

What remains is teardown on a timer: IMAP-import the six old mailboxes into
Fastmail, hold the IONOS mailboxes about 48 hours for a final delta pass, and
let the already-filed cancellation kill the contract before the renewal date.
The compromised-in-2018 SFTP password stops mattering the moment the contract
dies with it.

## The arithmetic

$221 a year became roughly $30 a year in domain renewals. DNS is free at the
registrar, and mail rides the Fastmail plan we already pay for. The migration
itself cost $24 in transfer fees and an afternoon. The archive, honestly, was
worth more than the savings.

## How this was actually driven

Most of the clicking wasn't me. My AI operator ran the recon, drove the
browser through the IONOS console and the Namecheap zone builder, mirrored
the webspace, wrote the runbook, and flagged the webshell. I stayed on the
things that should never touch an agent's transcript: EPP codes, payments,
and passwords. That split, agent does the inventory and the repetitive record
entry while a human holds the secrets and the go/no-go, is what made a
17-year hosting exit fit in one afternoon.
